## `sleep 1` is not one second

In Sonic Pi, `sleep 1` advances the musical clock by one beat, and that's all it
promises. `use_bpm` supplies the conversion to seconds. Your score gets to
describe relationships in musical time and leave the performance speed open.

You'll find durations much easier to reason about once you read them as symbolic spans.
Half a beat is half the pulse whether the pulse is crawling or sprinting. That's
why the same note and duration arrays run at 60, 96 or 152 beats per minute
without touching a single event.

This program plays one phrase at all three rates. Follow the duration pattern
before you judge the speed you're hearing: two half-beat notes lead into a full beat, then the
pattern answers itself.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_synth :fm

notes = [:c4, :e4, :g4, :a4, :g4, :e4]
durations = [0.5, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |pitches, lengths|
  pitches.zip(lengths).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.7
    sleep duration
  end
end

[60, 96, 152].each do |tempo|
  use_bpm tempo
  puts "#{tempo} BPM"
  play_phrase notes, durations
  sleep 2
end
```

At 60 BPM one beat lasts exactly one second. At 96 and 152, those identical
durations take progressively less wall-clock time. The slow pass leaves air
around every note, the middle one reads as a compact tune, and the fast one
starts to sound like a riff. Nothing in the arrays moved. Tempo changed the
physical scale you're perceiving them on.

## Change the rate, keep the shape

1. Drop the middle tempo and put 60 straight next to 152. Does the bigger jump
   make the shared duration pattern easier to hear, or does losing the middle
   step make articulation harder to compare?

2. Restore it, then double every duration *and* double the BPM. The phrase now
   occupies twice as many beats, and each beat takes half as long. Its
   wall-clock length barely moves while its relationship to the pulse changes
   completely.

3. Restore the score and change only the final duration to `2`. Global tempo
   hasn't moved, but the phrase now leans on its last note. That's a local
   change, and it sounds nothing like slowing the whole performance down.

## Why the indirection pays

Tempo is a conversion function. At `bpm` beats per minute, one beat lasts
`60.0 / bpm` seconds. Your score stays in beats and you never touch seconds and Sonic Pi's scheduler places
the events in physical time. At 60 BPM the conversion is invisible, since a beat
is a second. At 120 it's half a second.

That indirection is what gives your score a stable internal shape. `[0.5, 0.5, 1]`
always says two equal short events fill the same span as the long one that
follows. Pick a new BPM and the relationship survives. In programming terms,
your own duration array supplies values in one domain and tempo does the conversion
at the boundary.

The printed BPM and the sound are checking different things. The log confirms
which conversion is live. Playback tells you what that rate did to grouping,
articulation and character, which is the part you actually care about. A numerical mistake can still produce a plausible
phrase, so look at both.

Envelope times go through the same conversion. A release of half a beat lasts
half a second at 60 BPM and under a fifth of a second at 152. That scaling
usually helps, because fast notes get shorter physical tails and slow notes get
longer ones. If some later effect genuinely needs a fixed number of
milliseconds, make that an explicit exception. The moment beats and seconds
start blurring together, every tempo change becomes a debugging session.

Part 3 builds rhythm out of duration arrays and their sums. Before that fuller
treatment of time, Part 1 turns inward and asks why the same pitch can arrive in
so many different colours.

## Take it further

Write an eight-event phrase whose durations add to four beats, using at least
two different duration values so there's a rhythmic relationship worth
preserving. Play those arrays at 60, 96 and 152 BPM, and before each pass print
the expected physical length with `durations.sum * 60.0 / bpm`.

The sum fixes the score length; the calculation predicts the seconds. Compare
those printed numbers against the three performances in Sonic Pi 5, then write
down whether tempo changed only the speed or changed what the material *is*. A
spacious melody can become a compact riff with its internal proportions
completely intact.
